The problem

Most HR reporting time is spent before any thinking starts.

A compensation specialist spends a day and a half every month cleaning a spreadsheet before a single chart exists. Roughly four-fifths of that effort produces no insight at all — it is tidying.

The month-end tax

Dates in two formats. One department written three ways. Blank salary cells. Duplicate employee IDs. Every month, the same clean-up, by hand.

Definitions that drift

Two people calculate turnover, two different answers — because nobody wrote down whether the denominator is average headcount or end-of-period.

The unanswered question

The report lands, the CEO reads it, and asks: "So what do I actually do?" If HR cannot answer that, the dashboard was decoration.

"Chỉ số nào không nói được cách tính thì đừng đo."
If a metric cannot state how it is calculated, do not measure it. The governing rule of this build — from an HR practitioner's review of the metric set
The method

Eight stages, each with a human decision at the end of it.

The machine does the work. The human makes the calls. Nothing moves to the next stage until someone has signed the one before it — and that signature is recorded in the artefact, not in a chat window.

Nine sign-off gates on this engagement. A definition is signed before its measure exists; a report specification is locked before a page is built; the person who validates is never the person who built.

What that discipline buys you

  • Every number is answerable. Point at any figure on any page and there is a written definition behind it: the formula, the grain, the edge cases, and the person who owns what it means.
  • Definitions stop drifting. Turnover is calculated one way, written down once, and used everywhere. The denominator is stated on the visual itself.
  • The build is reproducible. Not a file someone hand-crafted and cannot rebuild — a versioned estate that regenerates from source.
  • What cannot be measured is written down too. The triage document records every metric considered, and for each one that was dropped, the evidence that killed it.

A countable inventory, not a slide deck.

The eight domains, and the questions they close

Workforce & cost

Headcount against plan, workforce cost as a share of revenue, cost per employee, and where the establishment is over or under.

Retention

Who leaves, at what tenure, for what reason, and which parts of the workforce carry the churn.

Talent acquisition

Fill rate, time to fill, where the funnel leaks, and which sourcing channels produce hires that stay.

Performance

Rating distribution, promotion and reward rates, and where performance sits against engagement.

Learning

Completion, cost, and whether training reaches the levels that need it or concentrates at the top.

Engagement

Engagement index and quarterly advocacy, by department — with the definitional distinction between the two stated, not blurred.

Compensation & benefits

Position against market by role and level, the pay gap raw and like-for-like, and whether the benefits budget is actually used.

Operations

Productivity by location and format, and a shortlist of sites meeting an explicit, printed intervention rule.

The report

Eight pages, each answering one question.

Every page title is the question its reader actually asks. Every visual on it exists to answer that question — and states the basis it is calculated on.

Six further pages sit behind these — three drill-through views for detail and three context panels that appear on hover.

Who it serves

Six readers. Six decisions. One estate.

A report earns its place by the calls it makes easier — not by the number of charts on it. Each page was specified against a named reader and the decision they open it to make.

ReaderOpens it to decide
Chief Executive Whether the workforce is on plan in size and cost, and where to add or hold headcount
HR Director Where retention effort goes, which parts of the workforce are actually churning, and what to put in front of the board
Talent Acquisition Lead Which sourcing channels to fund, and where the hiring funnel is losing candidates
Learning & Development Lead Where the training budget goes next, and whether delivery reaches the levels that need it
Compensation & Benefits Lead Where pay sits against market, whether the gap survives a like-for-like comparison, and which benefits are worth their cost
Operations Director Which locations to intervene in, against a rule printed on the page rather than held in someone's head
Why it holds up

Built to survive the room, not just to fill it.

An HR audience probes. The three commitments below are what let a presenter answer rather than deflect.

Every figure states its method

Each metric carries its formula and its denominator. Turnover visuals name the headcount basis on the page, because average and end-of-period give different answers and someone always asks.

Findings that are not there are said out loud

Where a relationship was tested and did not hold, the report says so plainly instead of implying one. A defended null beats a flattering correlation that collapses under questioning.

Provenance is on the face of it

A reader always knows which figures are measured and which are modelled. Nothing is presented as observed fact that was not observed.

Every number carries its comparison

No headline figure stands alone. Each one is shown beside its movement against the prior year or against plan, coloured for whether that movement is good or bad for that particular measure — so a reader sees direction, not just level, without asking for it.

Independent verification before anything reaches a page

Figures are re-derived independently and checked against the model before they are allowed onto a visual, and the person who validates the build is never the person who built it. The metric triage records what was measured, what was deliberately dropped, and the evidence behind each decision — so a reviewer can audit the reasoning, not just the output.

Three of the metrics originally requested were dropped after testing, because the data did not support them. That is recorded in the deliverable — with the evidence — rather than quietly omitted.
Working with us

What you bring, and what comes back.

What you bring

Less than most teams expect:

  • A data extract — a spreadsheet is a perfectly good starting point. It does not need to be clean.
  • The metrics you actually care about, or a conversation to work them out.
  • One person who knows the business well enough to say what a number should mean.

What comes back

  • A governed semantic model your team can build on, not a one-off file.
  • A report specified against real readers and real decisions.
  • A written metric dictionary — the asset that outlives the report.
  • Documentation of what can be measured today, and what data you would need to measure the rest.

The honest version of the pitch

No system purchase is required to start. What is required is a data extract that is good enough, a metric set with agreed definitions, and someone in the business who can read the result. The hard part was never the tooling — it is agreeing what the numbers mean. That is the part this method makes routine.

The metric dictionary — 102 governed measures

Every measure carries a written definition, its display format, and the basis it is calculated on. Where a figure rests on modelled rather than measured data, the definition says so. This dictionary is the asset that outlives any single report.

Compensation6 measures
MeasureFormatDefinition
Benefits Utilisation %0.0%Of the benefit lines employees are ENROLLED in, the share actually used. Denominator is enrolment, not headcount - utilisation of a benefit nobody is enrolled in is undefined, not zero.
Bonus % of Base0.0%Bonus paid as a share of accrued base salary cost - how much of total pay is variable. NOT a bonus participation rate.
Compa-Ratio0.000MEAN OF PER-EMPLOYEE RATIOS (not total pay over total market): each person's base salary divided by the market P50 for their own role, level and the last year in filter. 1.00 is at market; company-wide is 0.987.
Market P50#,0Market midpoint for the roles and levels in scope, in the LAST year of the current date filter. An unweighted mean across roles - read it at role-and-level grain, where it means something.
Pay Gap Like-for-Like %0.00%Gap remaining after controlling for JOB ROLE and JOB LEVEL, headcount-weighted across matched cells. +0.07% (z = +0.11) in this estate - indistinguishable from zero, so the raw gap is a REPRESENTATION effect, not a like-for-like pay effect.
Pay Gap Raw %0.00%UNADJUSTED gap: (mean male pay - mean female pay) / mean male pay. +4.8% in this estate.
Engagement2 measures
MeasureFormatDefinition
Engagement Index0.00Mean per-employee MONTHLY engagement score, 1-10. Distinct from eNPS in grain, scale and construction.
eNPS0.0Employee net promoter score, -100..+100, RECOMPUTED from promoter/detractor/respondent counts so it aggregates correctly across departments of different sizes. Quarterly grain - a month filter narrower than a quarter returns blank by design.
Learning10 measures
MeasureFormatDefinition
Average Course Score0.0Mean score on COMPLETED courses. Dropped and running enrolments carry no score and are excluded, not counted as zero.
Completed Enrollments#,0Enrolments with status Completed. Only these contribute training hours.
Cost per Training Hour$#,0.00Training cost over delivered hours. ASYMMETRIC BY DESIGN: the numerator includes seats paid for but dropped, the denominator counts only hours delivered - so a poor completion rate shows up here as an expensive hour.
Total Enrollments#,0All training enrolments in the period - completed, dropped and still running. DECLARED SYNTHETIC.
Training Completion Rate0.0%Completed enrolments over all enrolments. Still-running enrolments sit in the denominator, so a period ending mid-course reads low.
Training Cost$#,0Cost of the enrolments in the period, INCLUDING dropped and still-running seats. Seat cost only - no trainer time, venue or travel.
Training Hours#,0Hours of COMPLETED training, sourced from Enrollments x Course so the value is attributable /// to a course, category and delivery mode. 'Monthly Performance'[Training Hours] carries the /// identical total (706,086 for the full window, reconciled at the enrichment gate) but has no /// Course key, so a course or category filter silently did nothing to it.
Training Hours Share %0.0%The group's share of delivered training hours. Read against Headcount Share % on the SAME axis - that comparison is the training-reach finding.
Training Hours per Employee0.0Delivered hours divided by DISTINCT EMPLOYEES ACTIVE in the period (not average headcount). An average hides the distribution - it says nothing about how many people got zero.
Training Reach Gap pp+0.0%;-0.0%;0.0%Training reach against headcount weight, in percentage POINTS: share of delivered training hours minus share of headcount, per job level. Positive means a level takes more training than its size warrants; negative means it is under-served.
Performance8 measures
MeasureFormatDefinition
% Below0.0%Share of employee-months rated below 3.0. Band boundaries are a stated convention - no rating scale definition ships with the workbook.
% Exceed0.0%Share of employee-months rated 4.0 or above. The three distribution bands sum to 100%.
% Meet0.0%Share of employee-months rated 3.0 up to but not including 4.0.
Average Performance Rating0.00Mean monthly overall rating on the 1-5 scale, weighted by EMPLOYEE-MONTH not by person. No target is set - an open question for the HR Director.
Company Average Rating0.00The company-wide mean performance rating in the CURRENT date context, ignoring any department or employee slice. The comparison baseline for a per-department rating chart - bind reference lines to THIS rather than a hardcoded literal, which drifts the moment the rating distribution or the year selection changes.
Company Engagement Index0.00The company-wide engagement index in the CURRENT date context, ignoring any department or employee slice. The Y-axis baseline on the rating-vs-engagement scatter; its X-axis partner is [Company Average Rating].
Promotion Rate0.0%Share of EMPLOYEE-MONTHS in which a promotion was recorded - not the share of people promoted in a year. Multiply by 12 for a rough annual per-person reading, and say so.
Salary Increase Rate0.0%Share of EMPLOYEE-MONTHS in which a salary increase was recorded. The flag records that an increase happened; the AMOUNT is not in the estate.
Retail operations8 measures
MeasureFormatDefinition
Customer Satisfaction0.00Mean customer satisfaction score, 3.5-10 in this estate. A different scale from NPS - do not plot them on a shared axis.
Intervention Flag01 when a store is in the BOTTOM quartile of sales attainment AND the TOP quartile of /// turnover, both measured over the trailing 12 months ending at the last date in context. /// Quartile cuts are computed across the stores currently in scope, so the rule stays true /// under a slicer.
NPS Score0.0Mean CUSTOMER net promoter score, -100..+100. NOT eNPS, which measures employees - same scale, different subject, routinely confused.
On-Time Delivery %0.0%Mean share of deliveries inside their window. The source column stores percentage POINTS (80.6-100.0); this measure divides by 100.
Sales Actual$#,0Store sales for the store-department-months in scope. This IS the estate's Net Revenue - and it COVERS THREE OF NINE DEPARTMENTS (Fresh Produce, Meat/Fish & Bakery, Store Operations).
Sales Attainment0.0%Actual sales over target, across the three selling departments. 'Turnover Rate -> Sales Attainment' was TESTED across all 150 stores and is NOT SUPPORTED (r = +0.014, critical value 0.160 at n = 150) - the report shows that null result deliberately.
Sales Target$#,0Planned sales for the store-department-months in scope. Same three-department coverage as Sales Actual.
Waste %0.00%Mean product loss. The source column stores percentage POINTS (0.5-6.0); this measure divides by 100 so it formats as a true percentage.
Retention9 measures
MeasureFormatDefinition
Company Turnover Rate0.0%The company-wide annualised turnover rate in the CURRENT date context, ignoring any department, employment-type or tenure slice. This is the honest comparison baseline for a per-department or per-employment-type chart: headcount-weighted, so it is the company's actual rate rather than the unweighted mean of the plotted categories.
Early Attrition Rate0.0%Of the people HIRED in the period, the share who left within 365 days of their own hire date. Cohort-based, so the trailing twelve months are censored and read low.
Exits#,0People whose exit date falls inside the period. Exit DATE is source data; exit type and reason are DECLARED SYNTHETIC.
Involuntary Exits#,0Exits in the period the company ended - performance, redundancy, misconduct, or a fixed-term contract reaching its end. DECLARED SYNTHETIC exit type.
Probation Pass Rate0.0%Of the probations that CONCLUDED for hires in the period, the share that passed. 'In progress' is excluded from the denominator, not counted as a failure.
Turnover Rate0.0%ANNUALISED. BASIS: exits in the period divided by AVERAGE headcount - the mean of month-end headcounts across the months in the period, NOT end-of-period headcount - normalised to a 12-month basis by [Years in Context].
Turnover Rate PY0.0%Turnover Rate (average-headcount basis) for the same period one year earlier. Blank for 2022 - there is no 2021 in the date table.
Voluntary Exit Share %0.0%Share of the period's exits that the employee chose. NOT a regretted-loss rate - that needs a judgement flag the estate does not carry.
Voluntary Exits#,0Exits in the period where the employee chose to leave. DECLARED SYNTHETIC exit type.
Talent acquisition18 measures
MeasureFormatDefinition
Applications#,0Applications received in the period, read on APPLIED date. DECLARED SYNTHETIC.
Conversion Rate0.0%Hires divided by total applications. BASIS: numerator is dated by onboard date, denominator by applied date - at month grain the two are slightly different cohorts.
Cost per Hire$#,0Attributed sourcing cost divided by hires. Cost is dated by applied date and hires by onboard date, so read at year or trailing-twelve-month grain.
Days Open0.0Mean days a still-OPEN requisition has been open, measured to the 2024-12-31 data cut-off rather than a live today. Filled and cancelled requisitions are excluded.
Fill Rate0.0%Positions filled divided by positions requested, on the cohort of requisitions OPENED in the period. Recent months are structurally low (cohort censoring), and cancelled requisitions stay in the denominator.
Funnel Stage Count#,0Harvester over the DISCONNECTED 'Funnel Stage' dimension: returns the count for whichever /// stage the visual is showing. Without this a funnel visual cannot put five separate measures /// on one stage axis.
Hires#,0People who STARTED in the period - applications at stage Hired, dated by ONBOARD date via the inactive onboard-date relationship. Onboard date equals that employee's hire date exactly (estate invariant).
Interviewed#,0Applications that reached an interview, read on applied date. DECLARED SYNTHETIC.
Offered#,0Applications that received an offer, read on applied date. DECLARED SYNTHETIC.
Positions Filled#,0Positions on the requisitions opened in the period that reached Filled status - read on OPEN date, the same basis as Positions Requested, so the pair is a cohort. DECLARED SYNTHETIC.
Positions Requested#,0Positions on the requisitions OPENED in the period. Counts positions, not requisitions - a requisition may carry two seats.
Screened#,0Applications that reached a screen, read on applied date. Monotonically <= Applications by construction.
Time to Accept0.0Mean days from offer to onboard, over the applications that reached both. DECLARED SYNTHETIC.
Time to Fill0.0MEAN days from requisition open to offer accepted, over FILLED requisitions only. Mean, not median - the senior tail is long.
Time to Interview0.0Mean days from screen to interview, over the applications that reached both. DECLARED SYNTHETIC.
Time to Offer0.0Mean days from interview to offer, over the applications that reached both. DECLARED SYNTHETIC.
Time to Screen0.0Mean days from application to screen. The four stage durations do NOT sum to Time to Fill - they start at application, Time to Fill starts at requisition open.
Win Rate0.0%Hires divided by offers extended - the closing rate. Pending offers sit in the denominator.

Workforce17 measures
MeasureFormatDefinition
Average Base Salary$#,0Mean annual base salary per PERSON across the filtered population, active and exited. Not an accrual over months.
Average Headcount#,0Mean of the month-end headcounts across the months in the current period. THE denominator every turnover rate uses - not end-of-period headcount.
Base Salary Cost$#,0Base salary accrued over the employee-months in the period, at one twelfth of each employee's annual rate. The estate carries no salary history, so a mid-period raise is invisible.
Benefit Plan Cost$#,0Employer cost of a specific BENEFIT PLAN, from the benefits utilisation grain - the per-benefit-type breakdown that [Benefits Cost] carries only as a single total.
Benefits Cost$#,0Employer benefits cost across the employee-months in the period. Reconciles to the benefits utilisation lines to the cent.
Bonus Cost$#,0Bonus paid across the employee-months in the period.
Budgeted Cost$#,0Approved people cost for the store-department-months in the period. A flow, like actual cost, so it does sum across months.
Budgeted Headcount#,0Approved establishment for the LAST month in the period - a stock, never summed across months, so it stays comparable with the point-in-time Headcount. DECLARED SYNTHETIC.
Cost per Employee$#,0ANNUALISED. Total workforce cost per head, normalised to a 12-month basis by [Years in Context] so the figure is comparable whatever period is selected.
Employees#,0Distinct employees with at least one active month inside the period. Greater than Headcount by exactly the people who joined or left inside it.
Headcount#,0Employees on the books at the LAST day in the current date filter - hired on or before it, with no exit on or before it. Point-in-time, not average.
Headcount Share %0.0%The group's share of total headcount. Exists to be read against Training Hours Share % - the gap between the two is the training-reach finding.
Headcount vs Plan %0.0%Actual headcount as a share of approved establishment, both read at the same as-of month. Blank where no budget row exists - an absent plan is not a met plan.
Headcount vs Plan Variance+#,0;-#,0;0Actual headcount minus approved establishment, in people, signed - negative means under-filled.
Revenue per Employee$#,0ANNUALISED. COVERAGE: store sales divided by SELLING-DEPARTMENT average headcount (Fresh Produce, Meat/Fish & Bakery, Store Operations), normalised to a 12-month basis by [Years in Context].
Total Workforce Cost$#,0Base salary plus bonus plus employer benefits for the employee-months in the period. A FLOW - it sums across months.
Workforce Cost % of Revenue0.0%COVERAGE: numerator is the cost of ALL NINE departments; denominator is store sales, which exist for the THREE SELLING DEPARTMENTS ONLY (Fresh Produce, Meat/Fish & Bakery, Store Operations). Read as the total people bill against booked revenue, not as a departmental efficiency ratio.
Design systemone grid, one vocabulary
ElementStandardWhat it means in practice
Layout grid8 pxEvery one of the 177 visuals is placed on a single grid derived from the design tokens — title band, filter rail, KPI strip and two content rows in the same position on every page.
Filter rail280 pxOne control vocabulary throughout: one-tap tiles where a field has few values, dropdowns where it has many. A reader learns the rail once.
KPI tierT2Value, its variance against a stated reference, and a colour that reflects whether the movement is good — applied identically on every page.
Type ramp4 sizesFour text roles, no more: callout, title, header, label. Consistency here is what stops a deck looking assembled rather than designed.
Colourrole-boundGrey always means the comparison — prior year or plan. Good and bad are reserved for variance and status, never for categories.
RatesannualisedEvery rate is normalised to a twelve-month basis, so one month, one year and three years are directly comparable rather than three numbers on different scales.

Model design

A star schema: 22 tables — dimensions describing the business, fact tables carrying the events — joined by 34 relationships (32 active, 2 deliberately inactive for role-playing dates). Every relationship is single-direction from dimension to fact. None is bidirectional, which is what keeps a filter predictable and a number reproducible.

All 22 tables22 tables
TableRoleColumnsPurpose
BenefitDimension1The five benefit lines an employee may enrol in and use. DECLARED SYNTHETIC layer.
CostComponentDisconnected2The three lines a workforce cost decomposes into, for the prior-year-to-actual cost bridge. A DISCONNECTED dimension.
CourseDimension7One row per training offering (30), with its category, delivery mode, duration and seat cost. DECLARED SYNTHETIC layer.
DateDimension9Marked date table - one row per calendar day from 2022-01-01 to 2024-12-31, the fact window of the workbook. Built as a Power Query partition, never a DAX calculated table.
DepartmentDimension2The nine organisational units, conformed across every process. Only three carry sales targets - the coverage fact behind every revenue-per-employee denominator.
EmployeeDimension30One row per employee ever on the books, active or exited (8,797). Full_Name, Manager_Id, Manager_Name, Manager_Status and Store_Location are deliberately NOT loaded - documented in the source card
FieldParamDisconnected3—
Funnel StageDisconnected2The five recruitment funnel stages in their natural order. A DISCONNECTED dimension - it carries the stage axis; the five stage counts are separate measures.
Job Role & LevelDimension4One row per (job role, job level) pair used anywhere in the estate - the conformed position dimension shared by the workforce, recruitment and market-benchmark facts.
Recruitment SourceDimension1The eight channels a candidate can arrive through. Conformed: it filters both applications and the employees hired through each channel.
StoreDimension7One row per trading location (150), with its format and city. Store[City] is authoritative geography - employees.Store_Location disagrees with it for 7,199 of 7,500 source rows and is not loaded.

ApplicationsFact19FACT - one row per candidate application (24,797). DECLARED SYNTHETIC layer. Department, Job Key and Store Id are denormalized from the requisition so the recruitment facts hang off the conformed dime
Benefits UtilisationFact6FACT - one row per employee-month-benefit line (541,545). DECLARED SYNTHETIC layer; the per employee-month cost sum reconciles to monthly_performance.Benefits_Cost to the cent.

Modelling principles applied6 rules
  • Conformed dimensions. Department, role and level are modelled once and shared by every fact that needs them, so a slicer filters consistently wherever it appears.
  • Single-direction relationships only. Bidirectional filters make results depend on evaluation order; none is used here.
  • A marked date table spanning the full window, so time intelligence behaves predictably and period comparisons are exact.
  • Measures live in one home table rather than scattered across facts — the dictionary and the model agree on where a number comes from.
  • Denormalised at preparation time, not chained at query time, where a chain would create ambiguity between two paths to the same fact.
  • Disconnected dimensions used deliberately for ordinal axes and parameter switching, each documented as such.

This demonstration estate is synthetic throughout. Rows marked Generated come from a declared enrichment layer that extends the base extract into domains the source did not carry — recruitment, training cost, market benchmarking, benefits take-up. The distinction is documented per column and disclosed on the report itself.

Standards the build is held to

Delivery standards7 checks
  • Definition before implementation. A metric definition is written and signed before the measure that implements it exists.
  • Traceability. Every measure on every page resolves to a definition card; an untraceable number fails the build.
  • Stated basis. Any ratio names its denominator on the visual where the choice changes the answer.
  • Independent verification. Figures are re-derived against the model before they are allowed onto a page.
  • Reviewer is never the builder. Validation is performed by someone who did not construct the thing being validated.
  • Accessible by construction. Colour is never the only signal; every visual carries a text alternative describing what it shows.
  • Reproducible. The estate rebuilds from source; nothing depends on a manual step someone remembers.
